issues.item: Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not coherent with the stated trauma type. For a relief worker in a war zone, family-related comments could plausibly be relevant, but crash imagery specifically centered on cars hit by accident points toward a road-traffic trauma rather than war-zone relief exposure. The trigger profile therefore mixes two distinct trauma contexts without supporting items linking them.

issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies only partially fit the trigger/appraisal pattern. Avoiding social contacts can follow family-related shame or guilt, and avoiding authority figures can fit war-zone exposure, but the set does not clearly connect to the unusual crash-imagery trigger. This makes the coping profile look like it is addressing a different trauma configuration than the trigger items.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: Negative appraisals of intrinsic fault and failed role are plausible for a relief worker, but in combination with the crash-accident trigger they create a mismatched formulation: the appraisals imply guilt/responsibility and role failure in humanitarian work, whereas the trigger item implies a motor-vehicle accident trauma. These elements are hard to reconcile as one coherent trauma-linked profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
issues.explanation: The trigger profile is not well aligned with the trauma type. For a relief worker in a war zone, police and generic surveillance could be plausible, but recurrent 'cars hit by accident' imagery points toward a road traffic accident trauma rather than war-zone exposure, and no other items anchor this to the stated trauma context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Authority Figures: Being around people in authority or uniform
issues.explanation: Avoiding authority figures or uniforms is only weakly supported by the rest of the profile. The trigger item specifies police rather than military, aid command, or armed personnel, making this strategy feel trauma-mismatched for a war-zone relief worker unless other items supported detention, abuse by authorities, or checkpoint-related threat, which they do not.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'There is something about me that made the event happen' is not impossible, but in this profile it sits awkwardly with the other selected items. 'Failed Role' fits a relief-worker trauma well, but a strongly self-causal intrinsic blame statement is less coherent without memory or threat content suggesting a specific preventable mistake or personal causation. This creates a mild but meaningful formulation mismatch with the otherwise role-failure/ongoing-reactivity pattern.

vignette:
Minh is a 22-year-old Vietnamese-American undergraduate who, during a gap year before beginning his degree, volunteered with a humanitarian relief organisation operating in an active conflict zone. He had arrived full of purpose, trained in basic first aid and logistics, believing that his presence could make a meaningful difference. What he encountered over the following four months systematically dismantled that belief. Checkpoints were a daily reality - uniformed soldiers, weapons visible and sometimes raised, eyes tracking every movement of the aid convoy. On one afternoon that he returns to involuntarily and repeatedly, the convoy was stopped at a military checkpoint where the commanding officer, dressed in full combat uniform, moved slowly along the line of workers, scrutinising each face with an unhurried, deliberate gaze. Minh stood still, acutely aware of being watched, certain in that moment that he had no control over what would happen next. A local colleague was pulled aside. There were shouts. By the time the situation was resolved - through the intervention of a senior coordinator - Minh had been standing in the heat for over two hours, unable to act, unable to help, watching. He returned home six weeks later, and the world he came back to did not feel like the same one he had left.

He enrolled in classes the following autumn, but the university campus, which he had imagined as neutral ground, turned out to be threaded with the very things that pulled him back. Campus security officers in their dark uniforms, the occasional police presence during events, even the particular quality of being observed in a seminar room - these became the live wires of his daily life. When he noticed someone in uniform at the edge of his field of vision, or felt the attention of a figure of authority settle on him, his body responded before his mind could intervene: heart rate climbing, breath shortening, a tightening across his chest that he could not override. These triggers did not merely cause discomfort; they carried him back, sensorially and emotionally, to that checkpoint.

What made these moments especially corrosive was the interpretation Minh layered over them. He had come to believe, with a quiet and devastating certainty, that his body had become something working against him - that its alarm responses were proof of a fundamental brokenness rather than an understandable legacy of what he had witnessed. He was certain, too, that he could not stop bad things from happening to him; the afternoon at the checkpoint had confirmed what he feared was always true, that when it mattered most he was powerless. And beneath both of these ran the belief that he had failed - that he had gone to help and had stood there, frozen, while someone else was in danger. These appraisals did not remain abstract. They fed directly back into his sensitivity to triggers: because he believed himself broken and helpless, every uniformed figure became evidence, every moment of being watched a test he was already failing. The loop between what he saw and what he concluded about himself tightened steadily across the first year back.

To manage this, Minh restructured his life around avoidance in ways that accumulated quietly and then became undeniable. He stopped attending campus events where security staff were likely to be present. He began taking longer routes across campus to avoid the security booth near the main library. In seminars, he positioned himself near the door and kept his gaze downward, avoiding the eye contact that felt, in some way he could not fully articulate, like the beginning of being assessed and found wanting. Most significantly, he withdrew from the small group of friends he had known before the deployment. Seeing them meant being seen - as someone who had changed, someone who had not come back right - and that was a confrontation he could not yet manage.

By the spring semester his GPA had dropped and his academic advisor had flagged his absences. It was this - the concrete, documented evidence that his world was narrowing - that finally brought him to the counselling centre. What he most fears is that the person who came back is the person he now is permanently. What he most hopes, though he holds it tentatively, is that someone might help him understand why his body still believes he is standing at that checkpoint.
